It would honestly be a relief to me if the Moon can't be seen right now. I really hope it isn't visible!

I'm in Santiago, Chile at 2026-03-16 07:30 -03 (UTC-0300) (2026-03-16T10:30:00Z in UTC), at latitude -33.4489 degrees and longitude -70.6693 degrees. My astronomy app says the Sun's altitude is -2.898 degrees and its azimuth is 94.319 degrees, so it is below the horizon. It says the Moon's altitude is 28.227 degrees and its azimuth is 89.613 degrees, so it is above the horizon. The Moon is 8.04 percent illuminated, 32.867 degrees from the Sun, and 382363 kilometers away. The sky brightness is civil twilight, the sky is clear, and I'm an ordinary adult with normal unaided eyesight who knows roughly where to look.

Do you think I'd actually be able to spot it?

Based on the specific data you provided, **yes, you would almost certainly be able to see the Moon.**

Here is the breakdown of why it would be visible to you:

### 1. Altitude and Position
The Moon is at an altitude of **28.227 degrees**. In practical terms, this means it is well above the horizon (about a third of the way up into the sky). It is not "hugging" the horizon where atmospheric haze or buildings might block it; it is high enough to be clearly visible in an open area.

### 2. The "Civil Twilight" Factor
You mentioned the sky is in **civil twilight**. This is the period when the sun is just below the horizon, and there is still enough light to see objects clearly without artificial illumination. While the sky is bright, the Moon is a massive, reflective celestial body. Even in a bright twilight sky, a Moon at 28 degrees altitude is very prominent.

### 3. Phase and Illumination
The Moon is only **8.04% illuminated**. This means it is a **Waxing Crescent**. 
*   **The Good News:** Because it is only 32.867 degrees away from the Sun, it will be very close to the Sun's position in the sky. 
*   **The Challenge:** Because it is so close to the Sun, it will be very bright and "washed out" against the bright morning sky. However, because it is a crescent, it will have a distinct shape.

### 4. Visibility Verdict
Because the Moon is roughly 30 degrees up and the sky is clear, you wouldn't have to "hunt" for it. If you look toward the **East/East-Northeast** (Azimuth ~90°), you would see the glow of the approaching sunrise. Within that bright area, the thin sliver of the waxing crescent would be visible.

**Summary:** It is definitely "up" and "out." If you look toward the direction of the rising sun, you will see it.
